title: Operator habits
summary: The habits that keep a media buyer in the game long enough to get good: bankroll and risk rules, treating tests as tuition, clean records and tax basics, a routine that avoids burnout and a portfolio of honest results. This module closes School 1 and prepares you for The Operator.

lessons.title: Bankroll and risk
objectives: By the end you can define a bankroll and keep it separate from living money.
By the end you can size tests and a daily stop-loss so one bad run cannot end your business.
By the end you can explain why a profitable campaign can still run out of cash.

steps.p: Many new media buyers do not fail because they never find a winner. They fail because they run out of money before they find one. Managing risk is about staying in the game long enough to learn and improve.

d.b: Staying in the game is goal one
d.s: Winners come to buyers who are still testing

steps.say: Here's a truth about this business. Many new media buyers don't fail because they never find a winner. They fail because they run out of money before they find one. As the screen says, staying in the game is goal one. Winners come to buyers who are still testing. So managing risk is really about staying in long enough to learn and improve.

steps.p: Split your money into clear pots before you spend on ads. Your bankroll is the pot set aside only for traffic and tools. The other pots are never touched for ads, however good a campaign looks.
steps.more: If the bankroll reaches zero, you stop, review and rebuild it from income over time. You never borrow to refill it and never raid living money or the emergency fund. This one rule protects you from the worst outcomes in this business.
d: Living money|rent, food, family. Never for ads
Emergency fund|kept apart. Never for ads
Bankroll|only for ad spend and tools
steps.say: Before you spend on ads, split your money into clear pots. Look at the cards. Living money is for rent, food and family, and it's never for ads. Your emergency fund is kept apart, also never for ads. Your bankroll is only for ad spend and tools. And profit is taken out on a schedule. If the bankroll ever reaches zero, you stop, review, and rebuild it from income over time. You never borrow to refill it. This one rule protects you from the worst outcomes.

steps.p: A common rough guide is to risk only a small share of your bankroll on any single test, often 10% to 20% for beginners. It varies with your situation. The smaller the share, the more losing tests you can survive.

d.label: full tests a $1,000 bankroll covers at $100 each

steps.say: How big should each test be? A common rough guide is to risk only a small share of your bankroll on any single test, often ten to twenty percent for beginners. It varies with your situation. In this example, a one thousand dollar bankroll at one hundred dollars per test covers ten full tests, the number on screen. The smaller the share, the more losing tests you can survive.

steps.p: Example: the same $1,000 bankroll split into different test sizes. Bigger tests give faster answers but fewer chances. If your first five tests all lose, only one of these buyers can still run a sixth test.
steps.say: Here's the same one thousand dollar bankroll, split into different test sizes. Look at the bars. At five hundred dollars per test, you get two tests. At two hundred and fifty, four tests. At one hundred, ten tests. Bigger tests give faster answers, but fewer chances. Now imagine your first five tests all lose. Only the buyer at one hundred dollars per test can still run a sixth.

steps.p: Example: two buyers each lose their first four tests and win the fifth. Buyer A risked $250 per test and is out of money before test five. Buyer B risked $100 per test and is still running.
steps.more: Example, assuming each losing test loses its whole budget, which is the worst case. Buyer B's tests five and six each spend $100 and return $150, a $50 gain each: $600 + $50 = $650, then $700. Buyer A never gets to run test five. Same skill, different survival.
steps.say: This example shows two buyers with the same skill. Both lose their first four tests and win the fifth. Follow the lines. Buyer A risked two hundred and fifty dollars per test, and hits zero before test five. Buyer B risked one hundred dollars per test, drops to six hundred, then wins and climbs back to seven hundred. This assumes the worst case, where each losing test loses its whole budget. Same skill, different survival.

steps.p: A stop-loss is a daily limit on total losses across all your campaigns. Once you hit it, you pause new spending and review tomorrow. It protects you from bad days and from the bad decisions bad days cause.
steps.more: Example: bankroll $1,000 and a 5% daily loss limit. $1,000 × 0.05 = $50. If today's campaigns are down $50 in total, you stop adding spend and review in the morning. The percentage is your choice; 5% here is a starting rule, not a law. The Budget and kill rules module adds a weekly cap and a bankroll floor on top.
steps.say: A stop-loss is a daily limit on total losses across all your campaigns. Follow the equation: bankroll, times your daily loss percentage, equals your daily stop-loss. In this example, one thousand dollars times five percent is fifty dollars. If today's campaigns are down fifty dollars in total, you stop adding spend and review in the morning. Five percent is a starting rule, not a law. It protects you from bad days, and from the bad decisions bad days cause.

steps.p: Chasing means raising budgets or skipping your rules to win back money you just lost. It turns a small, planned loss into a big, unplanned one. When you feel the urge, stop for the day and review tomorrow with fresh eyes.

d.text: The urge to win it back fast is the signal to stop for the day.

steps.say: Never chase losses. Chasing means raising budgets or skipping your rules to win back money you just lost. It turns a small, planned loss into a big, unplanned one. As the warning says, the urge to win it back fast is the signal to stop for the day. Step away, and review tomorrow with fresh eyes.

steps.p: Ad platforms charge you now. Networks often pay weekly or monthly, and may hold a new affiliate's money longer. That gap means your bankroll must cover spend until payouts arrive, even when the campaign is profitable.
steps.more: Example: each week's traffic earns $250 in payouts, and the network pays each week about a month later. You are profitable on paper from week one, yet you need $800 of your own cash before the first payment lands in week 5. Profitable campaigns can still run out of cash. Ask your network about payment terms and holds before you scale.
steps.say: Here's why a profitable campaign can still run out of cash. Ad platforms charge you now, but networks often pay weekly or monthly, and may hold a new affiliate's money longer. In this example, you spend two hundred dollars a week, and each week earns two hundred and fifty, paid about a month later. Read down the last column. By week four, you've put in eight hundred dollars of your own cash, before the first payment arrives in week five. Ask about payment terms before you scale.

steps.p: Example of the questions to ask a network manager before you scale. The answers tell you how much cash you need to carry before money comes back. Ask in writing and keep the replies with your records.

messages.text: How often do you pay, and how long is the hold for new affiliates?
Weekly, net 30 for your first two months, then net 7.
What is the minimum payout, and which payment methods do you use?

steps.say: Here's an example of the questions to ask a network manager before you scale. In the chat, the buyer asks how often they pay and how long the hold is for new affiliates. The answer: weekly, net thirty for the first two months, then net seven. Then the buyer asks about minimum payout and payment methods: one hundred dollars minimum, by bank transfer or U S D T. These answers tell you how much cash to carry. Ask in writing and keep the replies.

steps.p: Paid traffic involves risk, but it should not be run like a bet. The difference is in the habits. An operator sizes risk, follows rules after losses and keeps records. A gambler does the opposite.

b.title: Operator habits
items: Stops when the bankroll says stop

steps.say: Paid traffic involves risk, but it shouldn't be run like a bet. The difference is in the habits. On the left, gambler habits: bets big to win fast, raises stakes after losses, keeps no records, and borrows to keep going. On the right, operator habits: sizes tests to survive, follows rules after losses, records every test, and stops when the bankroll says stop. Aim to be on the right.

steps.p: Write these five rules on one page and keep them where you work. Decide them on a calm day. You will need them most on the days you feel least calm, after a loss or a sudden win.
d: Bankroll amount, in a separate account
No borrowing to refill the bankroll
When and how much profit you withdraw
steps.say: Write these five rules on one page and keep them where you work. Your bankroll amount, in a separate account. Your maximum risk per test. Your daily stop-loss across all campaigns. No borrowing to refill the bankroll. And when and how much profit you withdraw. Decide them on a calm day, because you'll need them most on the days you feel least calm, after a loss or a sudden win.

steps.p: Put your risk rules in the same spreadsheet as your plans. Type the bankroll once and let formulas work out each limit, so a smaller or bigger bankroll updates every line. Read this tab before every new test.

blocks.value: Example. Starting rules; adapt them to your situation.

steps.say: Here's a walkthrough of a risk rules tab in your spreadsheet. You type the bankroll once, one thousand dollars in this example, and formulas work out each limit. Look at the highlighted line: max per test is ten percent of the bankroll, one hundred dollars. Below it, the daily stop-loss is five percent, fifty dollars, and the bankroll floor is fifty percent, five hundred dollars. Profit withdrawal is monthly. These are starting rules. Read this tab before every new test.

steps.p: These are the mistakes that end media buying careers early. None of them is about skill with ads. Each one is prevented by a rule you wrote on a calm day and keep on the worst day.
d: Bankroll mixed with living money|separate account
One big test|10% to 20% per test
No daily stop-loss|write it, then obey it
Scaling before cash returns|plan for payment holds
steps.say: These mistakes end media buying careers early, and none is about skill with ads. Look at each card. Bankroll mixed with living money? Use a separate account. One big test? Risk ten to twenty percent per test. No daily stop-loss? Write it, then obey it. Scaling before cash returns? Plan for payment holds. Each is prevented by a rule you wrote on a calm day and keep on the worst day.

steps.p: Keep a separate bank account or wallet for your traffic business. Payouts go in, ad spend and tools go out. You see at a glance whether the business is growing, and record keeping and taxes become much easier later.

d.text: One account for the business, one for your life. Move profit across on a fixed schedule.

steps.say: Finally, keep a separate bank account or wallet for your traffic business. Payouts go in, ad spend and tools go out. That way you can see at a glance whether the business is growing, and record keeping and taxes become much easier later. As the tip says, one account for the business, one for your life, and move profit across on a fixed schedule.

takeaways: Your bankroll is separate money only for ads and tools. Never refill it with borrowed or living money.
Size each test as a small share of the bankroll and set a daily stop-loss.
Platforms charge now and networks pay later, so plan cash for the gap.
lessons.action: Write your five risk rules: bankroll amount, maximum per test, daily stop-loss, no borrowing, and when you withdraw profit.

glossary.def: Money set aside only for running traffic and tools, kept separate from living money and savings.
The share of your bankroll you allow one test to spend. Smaller shares let you survive more losing tests.
A daily limit on total losses. When it is hit, you pause new spending and review later.
Raising spend or breaking rules to win back money just lost. It usually makes losses bigger.
When and how a network pays you, for example weekly, or monthly after a holding period.

quiz.q: Your bankroll is $800 and your rule is a maximum of 10% per test. What is the most one test may spend?
Why can a profitable campaign still run out of cash?
options: Profit on a dashboard is never real
Payouts are always taxed before you receive them
Ad platforms charge now while networks pay later
Networks never pay new affiliates
quiz.why: Spend leaves your account now, while payouts arrive on the network's schedule. Your bankroll must cover the gap.

quiz.q: You lost $120 today and want to double your budgets to win it back. What should you do?
options: Double them while the ads are warm
Open a new campaign with a bigger budget
Borrow to increase the bankroll
Stop for the day and review tomorrow
quiz.why: That urge is chasing losses. Stopping and reviewing keeps a planned loss from becoming a big one.

quiz.q: Your bankroll is $2,000 and your daily stop-loss is 5%. What is the stop-loss?
Which money belongs in your bankroll?
options: Money set aside only for ads and tools
Next month's rent
Your emergency fund
A loan from a family member
quiz.why: The bankroll is money you have set aside for traffic and can afford to lose. Living money, emergency funds and loans stay out.

lessons.title: Your testing budget is tuition
objectives: By the end you can write a testable hypothesis before a campaign.
By the end you can keep a test log that turns results into lessons.
By the end you can spot when a test has stopped teaching and started wasting money.

steps.p: School fees buy knowledge you could not get for free. A testing budget works the same way. A lost test is not wasted if you know exactly what it taught you. It is wasted when you learn nothing and repeat it.

d.s: Repeating the same mistake is waste

steps.say: Think of school fees. They buy knowledge you couldn't get for free. A testing budget works the same way. As the screen says, losing tests are tuition. A lost test isn't wasted if you know exactly what it taught you. It's wasted when you learn nothing and repeat the same mistake.

steps.p: The same $100 loss can be tuition or waste. The difference is what happens before and after the test: a clear question before launch, and a written lesson after it that shapes the next test.
steps.say: The same one hundred dollar loss can be tuition or waste. The difference is what happens before and after. On the left, waste: no question before launch, five things changed at once, no notes after, and the same mistake next week. On the right, tuition: a clear question before launch, one variable, a written result and lesson, and a next test built on it.

steps.p: Every test follows the same loop. Ask one question, guess the answer, test it with rules, record the result, write the lesson, then design the next test from that lesson. Each lap makes the next one cheaper.
steps.say: Every test follows the same loop. Follow the flow. Ask one question. Make a hypothesis, your guess at the answer. Test it with rules. Record the result. Write the lesson. Then design the next test from that lesson. Each lap around this loop makes the next one cheaper, because you're building on what you already know.

steps.p: A hypothesis is a short guess you can prove wrong. It names what you change, what you expect and how you will measure it. Without one, a result is only numbers, and you will read into them whatever you hoped to see.

d.text: Example: 'A how-it-works video will get a lower cost per sign-up than a static image in Kenya, judged with the rule card after 3 × target CPA per ad set.'

steps.say: A hypothesis is a short guess you can prove wrong. It names what you change, what you expect, and how you'll measure it. Here's the example on screen: a how-it-works video will get a lower cost per sign-up than a static image in Kenya, judged with the rule card after three times target C P A, cost per acquisition, per ad set. Without a hypothesis, a result is just numbers, and you'll read whatever you hoped to see.

steps.p: Keep one row per test. It takes two minutes and becomes your most valuable file. After twenty rows you will see patterns about your geos, angles and formats that no course can teach you.
steps.more: Example: $60 on video at $1.20 per lead is 50 leads; $60 on the image at $2.00 per lead is 30 leads. One test does not prove video always wins. It tells you what to test next: three different hooks in video format, in the same geo.
steps.say: Keep one row per test in a test log. It takes two minutes, and it becomes your most valuable file. Read the example. On fourth October, the question was video or image, changing only the format. Spend was one hundred and twenty dollars, sixty each. Video got a C P L, cost per lead, of one dollar twenty, against two dollars for the image. The lesson: video won in this geo. The next test: three video hooks. One test doesn't prove video always wins, but it tells you what to test next.

steps.p: Keep the log as one tab in your spreadsheet, one row per test, the seven fields as columns. Fill the question, hypothesis and variable before launch, and the result, lesson and next step when the test ends.
steps.say: Here's the test log as one tab in your spreadsheet, one row per test. You fill in the question, hypothesis and variable before launch, then the result, lesson and next step when it ends. Look at the two example rows. Video won in Kenya, then question hooks won. And the highlighted next test builds on both: three question hooks, video, in Kenya. See how each row feeds the next.

steps.h: Plan learning money by the month
steps.p: Plan your learning money for the whole month, not one test at a time. Decide how many tests you can afford and how big each will be before the month begins, then stick to the plan.
steps.more: Example: a $300 monthly test budget and $100 per test gives 3 tests this month. If the first two lose, you still have budget for the third, which should be built on what the first two taught you.
steps.say: Plan your learning money for the whole month, not one test at a time. Follow the equation: your monthly test budget, divided by the cost per test, equals the tests you can run this month. In this example, three hundred dollars at one hundred per test gives three tests. If the first two lose, you still have budget for the third, built on what the first two taught you. Decide the plan before the month begins, then stick to it.

steps.p: Each test needs enough budget to be judged. Work out the daily budget for one ad set that has room for 3 target CPAs of $20 over 5 days. Then check it fits inside your monthly test money.

d.task: Room for 3 conversions at a $20 target CPA over 5 days. What daily budget per ad set?

steps.say: Time for a lab. Each test needs enough budget to be judged. You want room for three conversions at a twenty dollar target C P A, over five days. What daily budget does one ad set need? Then check it fits inside your monthly test money. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: Example: in your first month you run 6 tests and spend $540 in total. Two make a small profit and four lose. If each test left one clear written lesson, each lesson cost about $90 of spend.
steps.say: Here's a way to see the cost of learning. In this example, you run six tests in your first month and spend five hundred and forty dollars in total. Two make a small profit, four lose. If each test left one clear written lesson, each lesson cost about ninety dollars of spend. That's the number on screen. Seen that way, a losing test with a clear lesson still bought you something.

steps.h: What a test can teach you
steps.p: Each test should answer a question in one area. Over time you build answers in every area for your geo and vertical. That collection of answers is what experienced media buyers actually have.
steps.say: Each test should answer a question in one area. Look at the cards. Angle: which reason to care works. Format: video, image or carousel. Audience: broad or specific. Geo: where the offer fits. Funnel: a direct link or a prelander. And offer: which one converts. Over time, you build answers in every area for your geo and vertical. That collection of answers is what experienced media buyers actually have.

steps.p: Example: cost per lead across one buyer's first seven tests, with and without a test log. With notes, each test keeps what worked before. Not every test improves things, and no result is guaranteed, but the line has direction.
steps.say: This example shows cost per lead across one buyer's first seven tests, with and without a test log. The line with a log trends down, from two dollars forty to one dollar sixty. The line without notes bounces around and ends close to where it started. With notes, each test keeps what worked before. Not every test improves things, and no result is guaranteed, but the line has direction.

steps.p: If you run the same kind of test three times and get the same bad result, the lesson has already been paid for. Change the question, the offer or the source. Paying again for a lesson you already have is the most common waste.

d.text: Three similar tests, three similar losses: stop and change the question.

steps.say: So when does tuition become waste? If you run the same kind of test three times and get the same bad result, the lesson has already been paid for. Change the question, the offer, or the source. As the warning says, three similar tests, three similar losses: stop and change the question. Paying again for a lesson you already have is the most common waste.

steps.p: These mistakes turn tuition into waste. They are easy to make when you are keen to find a winner fast, which is exactly when you should slow down.
d: Several variables|change one thing per test
Ending tests early|let the rule card decide
No written lesson|one sentence per test
steps.say: These mistakes turn tuition into waste, and they're easy to make when you're keen to find a winner fast. No hypothesis? Write one before launch. Several variables? Change one thing per test. Ending tests early? Let the rule card decide. No written lesson? Write one sentence per test. When you feel rushed, that's exactly when to slow down.

steps.h: Compliance: never test a rule-breaking ad
steps.p: Some buyers say they will test a misleading claim just to see if it works. That is not a test, it is a policy breach that can cost the account and mislead real people. Only honest variations belong in your log.

d.text: Never test fake claims, fake urgency or unlicensed geos. If a version would break policy or law, it is not an option to test.

steps.say: Here's a compliance point. Some buyers say they'll test a misleading claim just to see if it works. That isn't a test. It's a policy breach that can cost the account and mislead real people. Only honest variations belong in your log. As the warning says, never test fake claims, fake urgency, or unlicensed geos. If a version would break policy or law, it's not an option to test.

steps.h: Before you call a test finished
steps.p: A test is finished when every ad set has reached a decision on the rule card, or the test hits its per-test cap, and you have written the answer down. Use this list to close every test properly. Rules: Budget and kill rules module.
steps.say: A test is finished when every ad set has reached a decision on the rule card, or the test hits its per-test cap, and you've written the answer down. Use this list to close every test. Spend reached the planned amount. Tracking roughly matched across systems. The result is written in the log. One lesson, in one sentence. And the next test is decided. The full rules are in the Budget and kill rules module.

takeaways: A losing test is tuition when it answers a clear question and you write the lesson down.
Keep one test log row per test and plan test money by the month.
Three similar tests with the same result means the lesson is paid for. Change the question.

quiz.q: You spent $400 across 5 tests. What was the average spend per test?

options: Change the question, the offer or the source
Run it a fourth time
Double the budget

quiz.q: What turns a losing test into tuition rather than waste?
options: It was cheap
It ran over a weekend
The network paid anyway
You wrote down a clear lesson and used it in the next test
quiz.why: Tuition means you learned something specific and acted on it. Cost alone does not make it useful.

lessons.title: Record keeping and tax basics
objectives: By the end you can list the records a media buyer should keep and set up a monthly routine.
By the end you can tell revenue from profit and earned from received.
By the end you can explain the general principles of tax for affiliate income and when to ask a professional.

steps.h: If it is not written, it did not happen
steps.p: Records show whether you are really making money. They help you prove income to a bank or landlord and answer a tax authority. Good records take minutes a day. Rebuilding them later can take weeks.

d.b: Records are part of the job
d.s: Minutes a day, not weeks a year

steps.say: If it isn't written, it didn't happen. Records show whether you're really making money. They help you prove income to a bank or a landlord, and answer a tax authority. As the screen says, records are part of the job. Minutes a day, not weeks a year. Rebuilding them later can take weeks.

steps.p: Keep proof of every amount that goes in or out of the business. Most of it can be downloaded from the platforms and networks you already use, so the habit is mostly about downloading and filing regularly.
d: Ad spend|invoices and receipts from platforms
steps.say: Keep proof of every amount that goes in or out of the business. Look at the cards. Ad spend: invoices and receipts from platforms. Payouts: network statements and payment proof. Tools: subscriptions, domains and software. Exchange: rates and fees on conversions. And agreements: network terms and contracts. Most of this can be downloaded from platforms you already use, so the habit is really about downloading and filing regularly.

steps.p: Your daily sheet is the first record. One row per day per traffic source is enough to start. Fill it at the same time each day so it never falls behind and every number is fresh.
steps.say: Your daily tracking sheet is your first record. One row per day, per traffic source, is enough to start. Read the columns. Date. Source, like Meta or TikTok. Spend, from platform billing. Conversions, from the network. Payout earned, the approved amount. Payout received, the cash that arrived. And a note for changes made or issues. Fill it at the same time each day, so it never falls behind.

steps.p: Once a month, download the proof of what you spent and what you were paid. Menu names change on every platform and network, and we are not certain of the current ones; look for billing, payment activity or statements.

steps.title: Ad platform invoices
steps.text: In Ads Manager, open billing or payment activity and download the month's receipts.

steps.title: Network statements
steps.text: In the network panel, open payments and download each statement and payment proof.

steps.title: File them
steps.text: Save each file in this month's folder as date_source_type, such as 2026-10_meta_invoices.

steps.say: Here's how to download your records once a month. Menu names change, so look for billing, payment activity or statements. Tap Next to follow each step. First, ad platform invoices: in Ads Manager, open billing or payment activity and download the month's receipts. Second, network statements: in the network panel, open payments and download each statement and payment proof. Third, file them. Save each one in this month's folder, named by date, source and type, like the example on screen.

steps.p: Earned is what the network credits you. Received is the cash that lands in your account. They differ because of holds, rejected conversions, payment schedules and fees. Track both, or you will think you have money you do not have.
steps.say: Earned and received are different numbers. Earned is what the network credits you. Received is the cash that lands in your account. In this example, you earn twenty F T Ds, first time deposits, at thirty dollars this week, so the dashboard shows six hundred dollars. But you're paid about thirty days later, two F T Ds are rejected, so you get five hundred and forty, and transfer fees come off too. Track both, or you'll think you have money you don't.

steps.p: Revenue is everything that comes in. Profit is what stays after every cost. Many beginners quote revenue and forget tools, fees and currency losses, then wonder why their bank balance does not match their story.
steps.more: Example: revenue $1,200, ad spend $850, tools $60, transfer and conversion fees $40. Profit = $1,200 − $850 − $60 − $40 = $250. Use received revenue for this calculation, so you count only money that actually arrived.
steps.say: Profit is not revenue. Revenue is everything that comes in. Profit is what stays after every cost. Follow the equation: revenue, minus ad spend, minus other costs, equals profit. In this example, revenue is one thousand two hundred dollars, ad spend eight hundred and fifty, tools sixty, and fees forty. So profit is two hundred and fifty. Use received revenue, so you count only money that actually arrived.

steps.p: Example: using the numbers above, $250 profit on $1,200 revenue is a margin of about 20.8%. Tracking margin month by month shows whether the business is getting healthier, even when revenue jumps around.
steps.say: Using those same numbers, two hundred and fifty dollars profit on one thousand two hundred revenue is a margin of about twenty point eight percent. That's the figure on screen. Tracking your margin month by month shows whether the business is getting healthier, even when revenue jumps around.

steps.p: One row per month, with received revenue and every cost. Formulas do the profit and margin so you never round in your head. Add a column for money set aside for tax, using the figure your accountant gives you.

blocks.value: Example. Revenue = cash received, not earned.

steps.say: Here's a walkthrough of a monthly profit sheet: one row per month, with received revenue and every cost. In this example, September shows one thousand two hundred revenue and two hundred and fifty profit. October shows nine hundred revenue and one hundred and twenty profit. lessons.title: A learning routine without burnout
objectives: By the end you can plan a simple daily and weekly routine for media buying.
By the end you can name the warning signs of burnout and habits that prevent it.
By the end you can choose where to focus your learning in your first months.

steps.p: Media buying rewards people who show up every day with a calm routine. Staying up all night refreshing stats feels productive, but tired buyers make expensive decisions. Build a routine you could keep for a whole year.

d.b: A routine you can keep for a year

steps.say: Consistency beats intensity. Media buying rewards people who show up every day with a calm routine. Staying up all night refreshing stats feels productive, but tired buyers make expensive decisions. As the screen says, a routine you can keep for a year beats a week of all-nighters.

steps.p: Example: a routine that fits around a job or studies. Short checks at fixed times, a block for building and a block for learning. Apply your rule card only at the morning check, the same time each day, as the Budget and kill rules module teaches.
steps.say: Here's an example of a simple daily routine that fits around a job or studies. Read down the table. A twenty minute morning check of spend, results and anything broken. Ten minutes to update your log. Sixty to ninety minutes to build creatives, pages and new tests. Thirty minutes to learn, one lesson or some ad study. And a ten minute evening check. Apply your rule card only at the morning check, at the same time each day, as the Budget and kill rules module teaches.

steps.p: Once a week, step back from the daily noise. Look at the whole week's numbers against your targets, read your test log and decide the next one to three tests and their budget. Put it in your calendar.
steps.say: Once a week, step back from the daily noise. Follow the flow. Pull the week's numbers. Compare them with your targets. Read your test log. Pick one to three next tests. And plan the budget. Put this review in your calendar, so it actually happens.

steps.p: Answer the same five questions every week, in writing. Over months, your answers show how your decisions improve, where you keep breaking rules and whether the bankroll is on plan.
d: What did I spend and earn?
What is the one lesson of the week?
What are next week's 1 to 3 tests?
steps.say: Answer the same five questions every week, in writing. What did I spend and earn? Which rules did I break? What's the one lesson of the week? What are next week's one to three tests? And is the bankroll on plan? Over months, your answers show how your decisions improve, and where you keep breaking rules.

steps.p: Answer the five questions in one row per week. After a few months you can read down the column of broken rules and see whether you are getting more disciplined, which matters as much as the profit column.

In week forty one, there was one late edit, and the lesson was no changes after nine p m. After a few months, read down the rules broken column. It shows whether you're getting more disciplined, which matters as much as profit.

steps.p: There is no shortage of content. The best sources are close to real data and real rules. Treat anyone selling secret tricks or guaranteed income with suspicion, and test ideas on a small budget before you trust them.

Ad libraries and spy tools help you study angles, but never copy. Platform help centres explain policies and settings. A community lets you ask, share and compare honestly. And your network manager knows what converts on their offers. Treat anyone selling secret tricks or guaranteed income with suspicion.

steps.p: Beginners often jump between sources, offers and tricks every week. Pick one traffic source and one vertical for your first few months. Depth in one place teaches more than a little of everything, and your test log stays comparable.

steps.p: Example: ROI is profit divided by spend. $60 profit on $420 of spend is an ROI of about 14.3%. Put ROI next to the raw numbers so readers can check your maths for themselves.

glossary.def: A one-page write-up of a campaign: goal, setup, what was tested, results and the decision made.
A small collection of your case studies, test log, creatives and rules that shows your work.
Return on investment: profit divided by spend, usually shown as a percentage.
Showing only the best results, such as one good day, while hiding the rest. It misleads readers.

quiz.q: Spend was $420 and revenue was $480. What is the ROI?
Which belongs in an honest case study?
options: Only your best day
Spend, revenue, profit and the period
Revenue only
Screenshots edited to look cleaner
quiz.why: Complete numbers over a clear period let readers judge the result for themselves.

quiz.q: Before sharing a screenshot of results, what should you do?
options: Hide IDs and personal data and check your network's terms
Post it exactly as it is
Round the numbers up
Crop out the dates
quiz.why: Private data must be hidden, and some networks restrict sharing offer details or payouts.

quiz.q: Why include losing tests in your portfolio?
options: To look humble
They show your method and what you learned
Networks pay for losses
The law requires it
quiz.why: Clear notes on a loss show how you think and decide, which is what readers want to see.

quiz.q: Spend $300, 12 FTDs, payout $28 per FTD. What is the profit?

lessons.say_intro: In this final lesson of the module you'll build a portfolio of results. You'll write a one-page case study with honest numbers, share results safely, and plan your next thirty days. It matters because honest results, including losses, show people how you think.
lessons.say_outro: To recap: one page per campaign with goal, setup, test, results and decision, honest numbers for the full period, and private data hidden before sharing. Your task: write a one-page case study template with the five parts from this lesson, and fill in the goal and setup for your first planned campaign. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: Your bankroll is $1,500 and your rule is 10% per test. If every test loses its full budget, how many full tests can you run?

You spend $300 a week. The network pays each week's earnings four weeks later, so the first payment arrives in week 5 after you have paid for weeks 1 to 4. How much of your own cash must you cover first?
exam.why: Weeks 1 to 4 at $300 each is $1,200 spent before any payout arrives.

exam.q: Your daily stop-loss is $60. At 3pm you are down $65 and feel sure one ad set is about to turn. What do you do?
options: Pause new spending and review tomorrow
Raise that ad set's budget to recover faster
Move the budget to a new campaign
Lower the stop-loss for tomorrow and keep going today
exam.why: The stop-loss has been hit. The rule exists for exactly this feeling.

exam.q: In one test you changed the audience, the creative and the geo, and CPA improved. What can you honestly write in your test log?
options: The new creative is better
The new geo is better
Only that this combination did better; next test changes one variable
The audience caused it
exam.why: Three things changed, so no single cause can be named. The lesson is to test one variable next time.

exam.q: Revenue $2,000, ad spend $1,450, tools $120, fees $80. What is the profit?
Your network dashboard shows $900 earned this month, but nothing has reached your bank. What is the most likely reason and next step?
options: The network is a scam, so stop all traffic
Payment schedule or hold; check the payment terms with your manager
Your ad account is broken
You should count it as received anyway
exam.why: Earned and received differ because of schedules and holds. Check the terms; if payments stay late beyond them, raise it.

exam.q: A friend says affiliate income paid in USDT is never taxable. What do you do?
options: Keep records and ask a qualified tax professional in your country
Believe it, because crypto is outside the system
Convert it to cash to make it tax-free
Split it across accounts so it is smaller
exam.why: Crypto income is often still reportable. Rules vary by country, so ask a qualified local professional.

exam.q: You check stats about 40 times a day and broke your own kill rule twice this week. What should change?
options: Check even more often to catch problems
Delete your rules, since you do not follow them
Set fixed check times, keep the written rules and take proper rest
Move to a new traffic source
exam.why: Constant checking and broken rules are signs of stress-driven decisions. Fixed times and rest protect your judgement.

exam.q: A network manager asks for proof of your results before raising your payout. What is best to send?
options: A screenshot of your best day
A one-page case study with spend, revenue, period and private data hidden
Your ad account login
Revenue figures only
exam.why: Complete numbers over a clear period, with private data hidden, are honest and useful. Never share logins.

exam.q: Your per-test cap is $300. The test's net loss reaches $300 while one ad set has 1 FTD and "looks promising". What do you do?
options: Stop the whole test, review the notes and plan the next one
Keep only the promising ad set running
Raise the cap for this test
Move its budget to a new ad set
exam.why: A per-test cap is a stop line for the whole test. Stopping keeps money for a better-designed test; the promising ad set goes in the log as a lead for the next one.
